Acronyms 146

AAMI
Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation. The standards body for medical equipment and the sponsor of the technician credentials.
AAPM
American Association of Physicists in Medicine. The physicists' professional body, whose task group reports set the display and equipment test patterns a quality control program uses.
ABC
Automatic brightness control. The fluoroscopic feedback loop that holds image brightness by raising mA, kVp, or pulse width as the patient thickens.
AC
Alternating current. Mains power that reverses direction, 60 Hz in the United States and 50 Hz in much of the world.
ACI
AAMI Credentials Institute. The body inside AAMI that writes and administers the certification exams.
ACR
American College of Radiology. The body that accredits imaging facilities and publishes the phantoms and scoring that accreditation uses.
ADC
Analog-to-digital converter. The stage that turns a detector's analog charge or voltage into the numbers an imaging computer can work with.
ADT
Admit, discharge, transfer. The messages that tell every system who the patient is and where they are.
AE
Application entity. A DICOM node, identified by its application entity title, address, and port.
AEC
Automatic exposure control. Ionization chambers in front of the receptor that end the exposure once enough radiation has arrived.
ALARA
As low as reasonably achievable. The radiation safety principle: the least dose that still answers the clinical question.
ANSI
American National Standards Institute. The United States body that accredits standards developers such as AAMI.
AP
Anteroposterior. A projection in which the beam enters the front of the body and exits the back.
ARP
Address Resolution Protocol. The mapping between a logical address and the hardware address of a device on the same local network.
BF
Body floating (applied part). An applied part that touches the patient but not the heart, isolated from ground.
BMET
Biomedical equipment technician. The job title for the technician who inspects, maintains, and repairs clinical equipment.
BRH
Bureau of Radiological Health. The former federal office whose radiation-emitting product work now sits inside the FDA device center.
C-ECHO
DICOM verification service. The DICOM ping: it proves two nodes can open an association and talk.
C-FIND
DICOM query service. A query that asks another node which studies match given criteria.
C-MOVE
DICOM retrieve service. A request asking a node to send matching studies to a named destination.
C-STORE
DICOM storage service. The push that sends an image or series from a modality or workstation to another node.
CABT
Certified Associate in Biomedical Technology. The entry-level credential on the certification ladder, below the technician credential.
CBET
Certified Biomedical Equipment Technician. The general technician credential, the usual step before specializing in imaging.
CCD
Charge-coupled device. A solid-state sensor that turns light into charge, used in some digital mammography and camera chains.
CDRH
Center for Devices and Radiological Health. The FDA center that regulates medical devices and radiation-emitting products.
CF
Cardiac floating (applied part). An applied part isolated well enough for a direct connection to the heart.
CFR
Code of Federal Regulations. The published body of United States federal rules; imaging performance standards sit in title 21, part 1020.
CHTM
Certified Healthcare Technology Manager. The management credential at the top of the technician certification ladder.
CMMS
Computerized maintenance management system. The database of record for the equipment inventory, work orders, and maintenance history.
CMS
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The federal agency whose conditions of participation a hospital must meet to be paid.
CPU
Central processing unit. The processor that does the arithmetic of reconstruction and image processing on a console or workstation.
CR
Computed radiography. Cassette-based digital imaging: a storage phosphor plate is exposed, read by a laser scanner, then erased and reused.
CRCPD
Conference of Radiation Control Program Directors. Where state radiation control programs write their shared suggested regulations.
CRES
Certified Radiology Equipment Specialist. The ACI credential for technicians who service imaging equipment: 165 questions, 3 hours, offered in May and November.
CsI
Cesium iodide. The scintillator that converts x-rays to light in indirect digital detectors and image intensifier inputs.
CT
Computed tomography. Cross-sectional imaging made by rotating a tube and detector array around the patient and reconstructing slices.
CTDI
Computed tomography dose index. The dose in one slice spread over a defined 10 cm length, so radiation delivered outside the chosen slice is counted.
DAP
Dose area product. Dose multiplied by the area of the beam, measured by a meter under the collimator.
DBT
Digital breast tomosynthesis. Mammography that sweeps the tube through an arc and reconstructs thin slices.
DC
Direct current. Current in one direction only; what an x-ray tube needs across its cathode and anode.
DHCP
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. The service that hands out addresses automatically; a 169.254 address means it could not be reached.
DI
Deviation index. How far an exposure landed from the target for that exam: the technologist's dose feedback number.
DICOM
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine. The standard for medical image formats and for the network services that move them.
DLP
Dose length product. The computed tomography dose index multiplied by the length scanned, so it grows with how much of the patient was covered.
DMM
Digital multimeter. The bench meter for voltage, current, and resistance at the test points a service manual names.
DNA
Deoxyribonucleic acid. The molecule carrying a cell's instructions, and the target that makes ionizing radiation dangerous.
DNS
Domain Name System. Turns names into addresses; if the address works and the name does not, it is this.
DQE
Detective quantum efficiency. How much of the radiation reaching a detector becomes usable signal.
DR
Digital radiography. Direct-capture digital imaging: the detector reads out electronically with no plate to carry to a reader.
DSA
Digital subtraction angiography. A mask image taken before contrast is subtracted from the contrast run so only vessels remain.
DVM
Digital voltmeter. A meter dedicated to voltage measurement; the pre-reading voltmeter on a console is one.
EHR
Electronic health record. The longitudinal patient record shared across an organization, which the imaging report lands in.
EI
Exposure index. The number a digital detector reports to say how much radiation it actually received.
EMI
Electromagnetic interference. Unwanted energy coupling between equipment; it works in both directions in an imaging suite.
EMR
Electronic medical record. The clinical chart inside one organization, where orders begin and reports arrive.
ESD
Electrostatic discharge. A static spark that destroys or weakens electronic parts without leaving a mark.
FDA
Food and Drug Administration. The United States agency that regulates medical devices, including every radiation-emitting imaging system.
GFCI
Ground fault circuit interrupter. A device that opens the circuit on a small imbalance between hot and neutral, tripping at 4 to 6 mA.
GI
Gastrointestinal. The digestive tract, from mouth and esophagus through stomach and intestines to the rectum and anus.
GSDF
Grayscale standard display function. The DICOM display calibration curve that makes the same image look the same on every monitor.
HIPAA
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. The United States law protecting patient information, with privacy, security, and breach rules.
HITECH
Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act. The law that strengthened privacy enforcement and added breach notification.
HL7
Health Level Seven. The text messaging standard that joins scheduling, chart, and imaging systems.
HLD
High-level disinfection. The level of reprocessing required for a probe that touches mucous membranes.
HTM
Healthcare technology management. The department and the discipline that manage clinical equipment across its life.
HU
Heat unit, and Hounsfield unit. Two different units with one abbreviation: thermal loading on a tube, and density in a computed tomography image.
HVL
Half-value layer. The thickness of aluminum that cuts beam intensity in half; the practical measure of beam quality.
ICMP
Internet Control Message Protocol. The protocol that carries the echo requests and replies a ping uses.
ID
Identification. A patient identifier, a device identifier, or the photo identification a test center asks to see.
IEC
International Electrotechnical Commission. The body behind IEC 60601-1, the safety standard for medical electrical equipment.
IP
Internet Protocol. The addressing scheme that identifies every device on a network.
IT
Information technology. The department that owns the network, servers, and security an imaging department depends on.
kVA
Kilovolt-ampere. A thousand volt-amperes: the apparent power a supply must be able to deliver.
kVp
Kilovolt peak. The highest voltage across the tube during an exposure; it sets beam quality and strongly affects quantity.
LAN
Local area network. The network inside one building or campus, where modalities and archives usually sit together.
LAO
Left anterior oblique. An oblique position with the left front of the body against the receptor.
LED
Light-emitting diode. A diode that emits light; the indicator and display backlight of almost every console and panel.
LPO
Left posterior oblique. An oblique position with the left back of the body against the receptor.
mA
Milliampere. Tube current: the number of electrons crossing from filament to target each second.
MAC
Media access control address. The hardware address built into a network interface, which a switch learns for each of its ports.
mAs
Milliampere seconds. Tube current multiplied by exposure time: the single number that sets how many x-rays are made.
MDS2
Manufacturer Disclosure Statement for Medical Device Security. The standard form that says what a device stores, how it authenticates, and how it can be patched.
MF
Magnification factor. Image size divided by object size, equal to the source-to-image distance divided by the source-to-object distance.
MPPS
Modality performed procedure step. The DICOM service by which a modality reports that an exam started, finished, or was discontinued.
MQSA
Mammography Quality Standards Act. The federal law that sets mammography accreditation, inspection, personnel, and quality control requirements.
MR
Magnetic resonance. Imaging from the magnetic behavior of tissue in a strong field; also the labeling scheme for magnet room safety.
MRI
Magnetic resonance imaging. A superconducting magnet, gradient coils, and radiofrequency coils; no ionizing radiation and the field is always on.
MTBF
Mean time between failures. The average interval between one failure of a device and the next; the headline number of a performance report.
MWL
Modality worklist. The DICOM query that pulls scheduled patients and accession numbers onto the modality console.
NaI
Sodium iodide. The scintillation crystal in a gamma camera, which flashes light when a gamma ray is absorbed.
NCRP
National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements. The body whose recommended dose limits and shielding reports are adopted into law and used by physicists.
NEMA
National Electrical Manufacturers Association. The manufacturers' standards association behind focal spot tolerances and the home of the imaging communications standard.
NFPA
National Fire Protection Association. The source of NFPA 99 for health care facilities and NFPA 70, the national electrical code.
NIC
Network interface card. The network adapter and its link light, the first physical check in any connection fault.
NRC
Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The agency that licenses byproduct radioactive material, which is why nuclear medicine has its own rules.
OID
Object-to-image receptor distance. The gap between the anatomy and the receptor; the main driver of magnification and blur.
ORM
Order message. The message type that carries a clinical order from the chart to the scheduling and imaging systems.
ORU
Observation result message. The message type that returns a result or report to the chart.
OSHA
Occupational Safety and Health Administration. The United States agency for worker safety: hazard communication, bloodborne pathogens, electrical practice, and PPE.
OSL
Optically stimulated luminescence. A personal dosimeter type read out by stimulating the detector with light.
PA
Posteroanterior. A projection in which the beam enters the back of the body and exits the front.
PACS
Picture archiving and communication system. The archive plus the reading workstations: it stores, retrieves, distributes, and displays images.
PBL
Positive beam limitation. Automatic collimation that sizes the shutters to the receptor in use.
PDU
Power distribution unit. The panel inside a system that takes the incoming feed and splits it to the subsystems.
PET
Positron emission tomography. Imaging that counts pairs of photons emitted in opposite directions when a positron annihilates with an electron.
PHI
Protected health information. Patient-identifiable information in any form, including what sits in consoles, caches, and service logs.
PING
Packet internet groper. The command that sends echo requests to an address to prove the path and the host are alive.
PM
Preventive maintenance. Scheduled inspection, testing, and service meant to find problems before a patient or a schedule does.
PMT
Photomultiplier tube. A tube that turns a faint light flash into a measurable electrical pulse.
PPE
Personal protective equipment. The gowns, gloves, eye protection, and respirators a task requires, plus the lead a radiation task requires.
PSP
Photostimulable phosphor. The storage phosphor in a computed radiography plate that holds a latent image until a laser releases it.
QC
Quality control. The scheduled measurements that prove an imaging system still performs within tolerance.
RAID
Redundant array of independent disks. Several drives working as one set so the storage survives a drive failure and raises an alert.
RAM
Random access memory. Working memory, lost at power off, holding the study a workstation is reconstructing or displaying.
RAO
Right anterior oblique. An oblique position with the right front of the body against the receptor.
RC
Resistor-capacitor (circuit). A resistor and a capacitor together, whose time constant is the resistance times the capacitance.
RF
Radiofrequency. The radio part of the spectrum: the transmit and receive energy of magnetic resonance and a common source of interference.
RIS
Radiology information system. The department system that schedules exams, holds the worklist, tracks status, and routes reports.
RJ45
Eight-position modular connector. The familiar eight-pin plug on a twisted pair network cable.
RMS
Root mean square. The effective value of an alternating voltage: 0.707 times the peak.
RPO
Right posterior oblique. An oblique position with the right back of the body against the receptor.
RSO
Radiation safety officer. The person who owns a facility's radiation safety program and can stop unsafe practice.
SCR
Silicon controlled rectifier. A gate-triggered solid-state switch used to control alternating current power.
SDS
Safety data sheet. The standard document for a chemical: its hazards, handling, protective equipment, and first aid.
SI
International System of Units. The metric system the modern radiation units belong to: gray, sievert, and becquerel.
SID
Source-to-image receptor distance. The distance from focal spot to receptor; standard distances are 100 cm and 180 cm.
SMPTE
Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers. The broadcast engineering body whose test pattern is the long-standing visual check for a diagnostic display.
SOD
Source-to-object distance. The distance from focal spot to the anatomy being imaged.
SOP
Service-object pair. The DICOM pairing of a service with an information object, which says what a node can actually do.
SPECT
Single photon emission computed tomography. Nuclear imaging that rotates a gamma camera around the patient to reconstruct slices.
SSD
Source-to-skin distance. The distance from focal spot to the patient's skin; the fluoroscopic minimum is a federal limit.
Tc
Technetium. The element behind technetium-99m, the workhorse tracer of nuclear medicine.
TCP
Transmission Control Protocol. The connection-oriented transport that carries imaging and messaging traffic reliably and in order.
TEE
Transesophageal echocardiography (probe). An ultrasound probe passed down the esophagus to image the heart from behind it.
TFT
Thin-film transistor. The transistor array on a flat panel detector that reads out each pixel's charge.
TJC
The Joint Commission. An accrediting organization that surveys hospitals on behalf of the federal payer.
TLD
Thermoluminescent dosimeter. A personal dosimeter read out by heating the crystal and measuring the light it gives off.
TLS
Transport Layer Security. The encryption that protects data while it crosses the network, used on interfaces that support it.
UPS
Uninterruptible power supply. A battery-backed supply that carries a load through a power failure.
USB
Universal serial bus. The common port for keyboards, scanners, card readers, and removable media on an imaging console.
VAC
Volts alternating current. A voltage reading on the alternating supply side of equipment.
VDC
Volts direct current. A voltage reading on a direct current rail inside equipment.
VLAN
Virtual local area network. A logical network carved out of shared switches, often used to separate imaging equipment.
VNA
Vendor neutral archive. An archive that stores studies from many systems in a standard form.
VPN
Virtual private network. An encrypted tunnel; the controlled way a vendor reaches equipment from outside.
WAN
Wide area network. The network joining sites, usually over links leased from a carrier.

The exam itself 15

Certifying body
AAMI Credentials Institute (ACI), the credentialing arm of AAMI
Questions and time
165 multiple-choice questions in 3 hours, closed book; on-screen calculator and notepad only
Delivery and windows
Computer-based at Kryterion centers, travel up to 100 miles; twice a year, May 1 to 15 and November 1 to 15
The six domains
Anatomy and Physiology 7 percent; Public Safety in the Healthcare Facility 8; Fundamentals of Electricity and Electronics 10; Healthcare Technology and Function 25; Healthcare Technology Problem Solving 25; Healthcare Information Technology 25
Passing
A criterion-referenced cut score set by the modified Angoff method; no cut score is published
Results
Pass or fail on screen and by email within 24 hours; those who do not pass also get a scaled score and an analysis of performance
Fee
$410 member, $460 non-member; retake $355 member, $405 non-member
Retakes and recertification
60 days between attempts, three attempts in two years, then a one-year wait; recertify every three years with continuing education
Where the points are
Function, problem solving, and informatics are 75 percent; the first three domains are 25 percent
Pathway 1, education
An associate degree or higher in an electronics, technology, or science program plus two years of full-time BMET work
Pathway 2, military
A United States military biomedical equipment technology program plus two years of full-time BMET work
Pathway 3, experience
Four years of full-time BMET work
Radiology specialty clause
Full certification also requires at least 40 percent of work experience in the radiology specialty over the last two years, with 25 percent over the last five years
Candidate status
The degree alone, the military program alone, or two years of work alone earns candidate status, not full certification
Credential ladder
CABT entry associate, CBET general technician, CRES imaging specialist, CHTM manager; all four are ACI credentials inside HTM

Anatomy, positioning, and terminology 22

Anterior (ventral), posterior (dorsal)
Toward the front; toward the back
Superior, inferior
Toward the head; toward the feet
Medial, lateral
Toward the midline; away from it
Proximal, distal
Nearer the trunk or attachment; farther from it
Supine, prone, erect, recumbent
Face up; face down; upright; lying down in any position
Lateral decubitus
On a side, horizontal beam; right or left names the down side
Dorsal and ventral decubitus
On the back, or face down, horizontal beam crossing side to side
AP
Enters the front, exits the back; patient supine or erect facing the tube
PA
Enters the back, exits the front; patient faces the receptor, so less magnification
Lateral
Crosses side to side; the named side is against the receptor
Oblique: RAO, LAO, RPO, LPO
Body rotated between frontal and lateral, tube and receptor square. RAO right front to the receptor, LAO left front, RPO right back, LPO left back
Axial, tangential
Along the long axis of the part; or skimming a surface to clear other anatomy
Decubitus
Lying down with a horizontal beam, so air and fluid levels show
Sagittal, median (midsagittal)
Vertically into left and right; the median plane into equal halves
Midcoronal
Vertically into anterior and posterior parts
Transverse (axial)
Horizontally into superior and inferior parts; state the level
Orbitomeatal, infraorbitomeatal
Outer canthus of the eye, or just below the eye, to the auricular point (ear canal)
Glabellomeatal, acanthiomeatal
The glabella between the eyebrows, or the acanthion where nose meets upper lip, to the auricular point
T1
About 2 inches above the sternal notch
T2 to T3, then T4 to T5 disc spaces
The sternal notch at the jugular; then the sternal angle
T6 to T7 disc space, then T10
The lower end of the scapula; then the xiphoid tip
Column count
33 bones: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, coccyx of 4 fused

Radiation: quantities, limits, and protection 29

Exposure and air kerma
Roentgen (R), and 1 R = 2.58 x 10 to the minus 4 C/kg in SI units; air kerma in gray (Gy) is the SI replacement
Absorbed dose
Gray (Gy), or rad; 1 Gy = 100 rad
Equivalent dose
Sievert (Sv), or rem; 1 Sv = 100 rem
Effective dose
Sievert, weighted for radiation type and tissue sensitivity
Prefixes
milli a thousandth (mSv, mGy, mR), micro a millionth; 1 mSv = 1000 microsieverts
Occupational effective dose
50 mSv per year, and a cumulative limit of 10 mSv x age in years
Occupational organ limits
Lens of the eye 150 mSv per year; thyroid, skin, hands, and feet 500 mSv per year
Public
1 mSv per year frequent exposure, 5 mSv infrequent
Embryo or fetus
5 mSv over the gestation; 0.5 mSv in any month once declared
Education and training, under 18
1 mSv per year
Natural background
About 3 mSv per year, radon the largest part; one chest image about 0.02 mSv
Time, distance, shielding
Dose rises with beam-on time; distance is the strongest control, so one step back beats any apron; shielding is aprons, mobile shields, the booth barrier, and lead in the walls
Inverse square law
I1 / I2 = (d2 / d1) squared. Double the distance, one quarter the intensity. Halving a fluoroscope's skin distance from 40 cm to 20 cm raises entrance exposure about four times
ALARA
As low as reasonably achievable: lowest technique, smallest field, fewest exposures
Aprons and gloves
0.25, 0.5, and 1 mm lead equivalent; at least 0.25 mm Pb required, 0.5 mm Pb normal. At 75 kVp, 0.25 mm Pb attenuates about 66 percent and 1 mm Pb about 99 percent, but 1 mm can weigh 12 kg (25 lb)
Thyroid and gonadal shields
Used and inspected like an apron; read the lead equivalent marked on the garment
Inspection and retirement
Fluoroscope or radiograph every apron, glove, and shield at least yearly, or use 120 kVp at 10 mAs radiography; replace on cracks, tears, or holes; store on racks
Gonadal shielding practice
Cuts ovary dose about 50 percent, testicular about 95 percent; use within about 0.5 cm of the primary beam. Flat contact shields lie on the patient, shadow shields hang in the beam
Bucky slot cover and curtain
Each at least 0.25 mm Pb equivalent; the cover closes the roughly 5 cm gap at gonadal level
Barriers and mobile work
The fluoroscopic receptor assembly is a primary barrier of at least 2 mm Pb, interlocked so the tube cannot energize parked; the booth is about 1/16 inch lead equivalent; a mobile switch must reach 2 m from the tube
Tabletop intensity
Not above 10 R/min (100 mGy/min) without high-level control, 20 R/min (200 mGy/min) with it, and not above 2.1 R/min (21 mGy/min) per mA at 80 kVp. No limit while recording
Cumulative timer
Audible signal at 5 minutes of beam-on time; record beam-on time every exam
Minimum source-to-skin distance (SSD)
Not less than 38 cm stationary, not less than 30 cm mobile
Control, filtration, collimation
Dead-man control stops the beam on release; total filtration at least 2.5 mm Al equivalent; an unexposed border must show with the input phosphor 35 cm above the tabletop
Zones
Zone I public, Zone II reception and screening, Zone III controlled and badged, Zone IV the magnet room
Field and the 5-gauss line
1 T = 10,000 gauss, a common magnet is 3 T, the field is never off. The posted 5-gauss line marks where an implant or pacemaker can be disturbed, so screening happens before it
Projectiles and screening
Any ferromagnetic tool, cylinder, or cart becomes a missile; screen every person and item every time. Labels are MR Safe, MR Conditional, or MR Unsafe
Quench and cryogens
Loss of superconduction boils off the cryogen; the quench pipe vents outside, a room-side release displaces oxygen. Liquid helium boils at 4 K, nitrogen at 77 K
RF energy and EMI
Deposited RF heats tissue, so looped leads and damaged coils cause burns. The scanner also interferes with nearby monitors and pumps, and a noisy device spoils the image

Regulators, standards, and what each asks for 18

FDA
Regulates devices and radiation-emitting products through CDRH, which carries the work the former BRH began; publishes the standards in 21 CFR 1020 and runs recalls and device reporting
State radiation control programs
Register every tube, inspect rooms, set operator and posting rules; CRCPD is where those programs write their shared suggested regulations
NRC
Licenses byproduct radioactive material, so nuclear medicine carries its own license, surveys, and records
CMS and TJC
CMS sets the conditions of participation and may survey directly; The Joint Commission surveys environment of care, asking for the inventory, maintenance strategy, PM completion, test records, and inspection history
MQSA and ACR
Federal mammography law under the FDA: accreditation, annual inspection, an annual medical physicist survey, personnel qualifications, a written QC program. ACR accredits facilities and publishes the phantoms
OSHA
Worker safety: hazard communication, bloodborne pathogens, electrical practice, and the PPE the employer must supply
ANSI and AAMI
The equipment-management standards a technology program is written against; ANSI accredits the process, AAMI writes the content
NCRP and NEMA
NCRP publishes the dose limits and shielding reports barriers are designed from; NEMA carries manufacturer standards such as focal spot tolerances
Tube housing leakage radiation
Less than 100 mR/h (about 1 mGy/h) at 1 m from the housing
AEC backup timer
Must end the exposure at 6 s or 600 mAs, whichever comes first
Light field to x-ray field
Within 2 percent of the SID; at a 100 cm SID that is 2 cm
Console and geometry indicators
PBL within 2 percent of the SID, the SID indicator within 2 percent, and the console must show exposure conditions and that the tube is energized
Minimum total filtration
At least 2.5 mm Al above 70 kVp, 1.5 mm Al from 50 to 70 kVp, 0.5 mm Al below 50 kVp
Equipment inventory
Every device by control number, model, serial number, location, risk class, and interval; the first thing a surveyor asks for
Work order
Who, what, when, the symptom in the caller's words, the finding, parts, labor, and readings after the repair
PM due list
What is due, what is overdue, and the completion rate by area
Service history and recalls
Every visit on a device, vendor reports included, so repeat failures show; plus which devices a notice touches and what was done
Compliance and performance reports
PM completion, failures, downtime, and cost per device for management review

Electricity, electronics, and imaging power 43

Ohm's law
V = I x R; I = V / R; R = V / I
Power
P = V x I; P = I squared x R; P = V squared / R, in watts
Series and parallel
Series: one path, resistances add, same current, voltages add. Parallel: several paths, reciprocals add, same voltage, branch currents add
Imaging system power rating
(mA x kVp) / 1000 = kW, so 1,000 mA at 120 kVp is 120 kW; multiply by 0.7 single phase
Transformer turns and AC values
Secondary voltage = primary voltage x turns ratio, so 120 V at 750:1 gives 90 kVp. RMS = 0.707 x peak, peak = 1.414 x RMS; mains is 120 V RMS at 60 Hz
kilo, milli, micro
A thousand, a thousandth, a millionth: kV and kW, mA and ms, and the microamps leakage limits use
kVp, mA, and mAs
Kilovolt peak is the highest voltage across the tube and sets quality; mA is tube current and sets quantity; mAs is mA x exposure time in seconds, the one number that sets how many x-rays are made
Resistor, capacitor, inductor
A resistor limits current and drops voltage, and sets mA in the filament circuit. A capacitor stores charge, smooths rectified voltage, passes AC and blocks DC. An inductor opposes a change in current: transformers, chokes, stator windings
Transformer
Changes AC voltage by turns ratio: autotransformer sets kVp, step-up makes kilovolts, step-down heats the filament
Diode and rectifier
A diode conducts one way, about 0.7 V forward drop in silicon; a rectifier set makes the one-way current the tube needs
Transistor and SCR
A transistor switches or amplifies on a small control current; an SCR is a gate-triggered AC switch used in primary circuits and rotor drives
Fuse, breaker, relay, contactor
Fuses and breakers open on overcurrent, and a repeat trip is a fault, not a nuisance; a relay or contactor lets a small coil current switch the rotor or exposure load
Interlock and indicators
An interlock sits in series with the exposure circuit: door, rotor ready, receptor parked, collimator, emergency stop. An unlit LED means the lamp or its drive is dead
Three-phase distribution
Facility power distribution for imaging is three-phase, commonly 480 VAC, stepped down to what each room needs; three-phase service feeds the larger generators
Single-phase service
120/240 VAC at 60 Hz with a grounded center neutral; most imaging systems are designed for 220 V, some 110 V or 440 V
Dedicated feed, disconnect, ground
Each room has its own feeder and a lockable disconnect: tag it before opening a cabinet. A lifted ground gives a leakage failure and image noise at once
Line voltage compensation
Building power is never steady enough for repeatable exposures; the compensator corrects the supply ahead of the autotransformer
Transformers in the generator
The autotransformer is a tapped winding the kVp selector picks taps on, read by a pre-reading voltmeter; the step-up secondary carries 500 to 1,000 turns per primary turn; the filament step-down supplies about 4 A or more
Low-voltage rails
Logic and interlock boards run on VDC rails from the cabinet supplies; measure each at the test point the manual names before condemning a board
Single phase, half-wave and full-wave
Half-wave passes only the positive half of each cycle, the least efficient; full-wave uses both halves at twice the pulse rate. Ripple is 100 percent either way, and without rectification the negative half-cycle would destroy the tube
Three phase, six pulse
About 14 percent ripple, so voltage never drops below about 86 percent of peak
Three phase, twelve pulse
About 4 percent ripple, never below about 96 percent of peak
High frequency
About 1 percent ripple, nearly constant voltage: most efficient and now standard. Less ripple means more quantity and quality for the same settings, so one technique is not the same exposure on another generator
UPS types
Online double conversion always runs the load from the inverter, the cleanest protection for consoles and archives; line-interactive regulates and switches on loss; standby only switches. Batteries age out
Line conditioner
Regulates and filters without a battery: cures noise and sag, not a blackout
Isolation and surge protection
An isolation transformer clears ground loops and noise; surge devices clamp transients. A surge strip is not a UPS
Internal distribution and brownouts
One feed splits to generator, gantry, table, and computers, so one branch can look like total failure. Low line voltage makes a generator read kVp low, abort exposures, or throw a line-compensation fault
Where they are and what is in them
Ultrasound carts and portable x-ray units, on sealed lead-acid or lithium-ion packs; never substitute a chemistry the unit was not built for
Charge before use
Leave the unit on the charger between cases; a lead-acid pack left discharged sulfates and will not come back
Capacity fade
Run time and exposures per charge fall with age; log them, because the trend is the warning
What a weak pack does
Low or aborted exposures, resets mid-exposure, or a rotor that will not spin; measure the pack under load
1 mA
Threshold of perception (tingle)
5 mA
Accepted maximum harmless current
10 to 20 mA
Let-go threshold: muscles contract and the person cannot release
50 mA
Pain, possible fainting, respiratory arrest
100 to 300 mA
Ventricular fibrillation likely
6 A and above
Sustained heart contraction, burns, respiratory paralysis
Microshock
As little as 10 microamps delivered directly to the heart (through a catheter or pacing wire) can cause fibrillation
Ground (chassis to plug ground pin) resistance
0.5 ohm maximum for patient-care equipment
Chassis (touch) leakage, cord-connected patient-care equipment
500 microamps in current editions (older editions used 300 or 100 microamps; know the limit your facility cites)
Patient care vicinity
About 6 feet (1.8 m) beyond the bed or chair and 7.5 feet (2.3 m) above the floor
GFCI trip
4 to 6 mA (nominal 5 mA)
Applied part types
Type B touches the body but not the heart; BF is body floating and isolated; CF is cardiac floating, safe for a direct heart connection

X-ray production, tubes, and generators 33

Cathode
A thoriated tungsten filament, 1 to 2 percent thorium, coiled about 1 to 2 cm long and 2 mm across, in a negatively charged focusing cup; two filaments give the small and large spots
Anode
A tungsten-rhenium target disc backed by molybdenum or graphite. Tungsten is chosen for atomic number 74, conductivity close to copper, and a melting point of about 3,400 C
Rotor and stator
An induction motor spins the anode, about 3,400 rpm standard and about 10,000 rpm high-speed; reversing the stator field brakes it
Anode angle and line focus
Angles about 5 to 20 deg. Angling shortens a long focal track into a small effective spot, so a 10 mm by 1 mm line becomes about a 1 mm square; smaller angle, smaller spot, stronger heel effect
Heel effect
Intensity is lower on the anode side because those x-rays cross more target material; put thick anatomy under the cathode side
Focal spot sizes
Small stations about 0.3 to 0.6 mm, large about 1.0 to 1.2 mm, mammography down to 0.1 mm. Nominal sizes carry a variance, so a nominal 0.3 mm may measure 0.45 mm and pass
Envelope, oil, housing
A glass or metal vacuum envelope; tungsten plating glass causes arcing, so metal lasts longer. Oil carries heat to the lead-lined housing, which limits leakage and shock risk
Efficiency
About 1 percent of the electrons' kinetic energy becomes x-rays, about 99 percent heat
Bremsstrahlung and characteristic radiation
Electrons braked by the nuclear field emit a continuous spread of energies, the bulk of the beam. An inner-shell vacancy filled from an outer shell instead emits a photon at exactly the difference in binding energies, and only K-shell transitions in tungsten are useful, above its K-shell energy of about 69.5 keV
kVp
Sets penetrability (quality, measured as the HVL) and contrast; quantity is proportional to kVp squared
mA and time
Both linear with quantity; short times freeze motion
mAs and reciprocity
mAs = mA x seconds, and any pair giving the same product should give the same receptor exposure, which is what the linearity test checks
The 15 percent rule
Raising kVp 15 percent equals doubling the mAs; to hold receptor exposure, raise kVp 15 percent and halve the mAs, accepting lower contrast
Filtration
Removes low-energy photons that only dose the patient: average energy and HVL rise, quantity falls
Distance and magnification
Receptor exposure falls with the square of the SID. MF = SID / SOD, about 1.1 at a 100 cm SID and 1.05 at 180 cm
Heat units
Single phase HU = kVp x mA x s, so 98 kVp at 120 mAs is 11,760 HU; three phase or high frequency HU = 1.4 x kVp x mA x s, because lower ripple makes more heat. 1 HU = 1.4 joules
Rating and cooling charts
The rating chart says whether one exposure is safe; anode and housing cooling curves say how long to wait before the next series
How heat leaves
Radiation from the anode, conduction into envelope and oil, convection in the oil to the housing, then the room. The anode is hottest for only about 1 to 3 seconds per exposure
Filament evaporation
Tungsten boils off, thins the coil, and plates the envelope; output drifts low, then the filament opens
Anode pitting and melting
Repeated overload roughens the target; output falls and becomes unpredictable across stations
Cracked anode
A cold anode loaded hard cracks or wobbles and fails at once, which is why the warm-up series exists
Arcing
Tungsten plated inside a glass envelope conducts, so tube current jumps the vacuum and the generator throws an overcurrent or tube-arc fault
Bearing wear
Heat into the rotor ruins the bearings: a noisy or slow rotor, then a rotor-fault lockout. Long fluoroscopic runs are hardest on them
Overheating
The most common cause of early failure. Lowest technique that works, fewest repeats, never exceed the rating chart; a well-used tube gives at least about 50,000 exposures
kVp and mA selectors
kVp picks autotransformer taps, mA sets filament heating; verify with a meter, not the display, and keep adjacent mA stations within 10 percent
Time and mAs
Timer types: synchronous (multiples of 1/60 s), electronic (common and most accurate), mechanical (portables and dental), mAs, and automatic
AEC and backup timer
Ionization chambers in front of the receptor end the exposure when enough radiation arrives; cell selection and density steps tune it, and the backup must end at 6 s or 600 mAs
Line compensation
Holds the supply steady so one technique gives the same exposure all day
Rotor, ready, and interlocks
First stage spins the anode and heats the filament, and the ready light means the interlock chain is satisfied. A two-stage dead-man switch sits in series with those interlocks, so an open link gives no exposure and no fault code
Collimator and PBL
Two pairs of lead shutters at right angles plus lamp and mirror, with cones and aperture diaphragms to restrict further. Light field and x-ray field must match within 2 percent of the SID, and positive beam limitation must hold the same 2 percent
Grid ratio, frequency, types
Ratio is strip height over gap, usually 4:1 to 16:1; frequency is strips per inch, usually 60 to 150; higher ratio removes more scatter and costs more dose. Linear grids are parallel, focused grids are angled with the labeled side to the tube, crossed grids are two at right angles
Bucky factor
The mAs increase a grid costs, also called the grid conversion factor; it rises with ratio and with kVp. Contrast improvement factors run 1.5 to 2.5
Air gap and compensating filters
A long OID lets scatter miss the receptor instead of using a grid, at the cost of magnification; wedge and trough filters even out a part that changes thickness

Receptors, fluoroscopy, mammography, CT, ultrasound, nuclear medicine, MRI 37

CR, and the film it replaced
A PSP plate stores the latent image, a laser scanner reads the glow, a bright lamp erases it for reuse. Dust and scratches print on every image, an incomplete erase leaves a ghost, a worn plate loses speed. Film vocabulary survives in questions: optical density, screen speed, screen-film contact
DR, indirect and direct
Indirect panels use a CsI scintillator over an amorphous silicon TFT array; direct panels use amorphous selenium, with no light step
DQE, EI, and DI
Detective quantum efficiency is how much of the radiation reaching the detector becomes usable signal, so higher means the same image at less dose. The exposure index reports what the detector received, and the deviation index compares it with the target for that exam
Calibration and care
Offset (dark), gain (flat-field), and defective pixel map; skipping them shows as banding, shading, or stuck pixels. Inspect portable panel cases and cables, and handle boards with ESD precautions
Image intensifier chain
Input phosphor, photocathode, electrostatic focusing lenses, anode, output phosphor; output phosphors about 2.5 or 5 cm, input phosphors 10 to 40 cm
Gains
Flux gain is the 50 to 75 light photons each photoelectron makes at the output phosphor; minification gain is the square of input over output diameter; brightness gain = minification gain x flux gain
ABC and magnification
Automatic brightness control holds brightness by raising mA, kVp, or pulse width as the patient thickens, so dose rate climbs on a large patient. A magnification mode uses less of the phosphor, so dose rate rises again
Flat-panel fluoroscopy
A dynamic flat detector instead of an intensifier tube: even brightness, no vignetting or S-distortion
Pulsed mode and last-image hold
Short pulses at a chosen rate are the biggest dose saving the operator has; last-image hold freezes the final frame with the beam off
DSA
A mask image taken before contrast is subtracted from the contrast run so only vessels remain; any motion ruins it
C-arm and the suite
A mobile or fixed C-arm adds its own collimator, laser aimers, brakes, detents, cables, and foot switches to the PM list
Targets, filters, technique
Molybdenum, rhodium, or tungsten targets with matching molybdenum or rhodium filters shift the spectrum into the useful range for soft tissue. About 23 to 28 kVp, with total filtration at least 0.5 mm Al equivalent through a beryllium window
Focal spot and geometry
Focal spots down to about 0.1 mm for microcalcifications; the cathode faces the chest wall so the heel effect evens out thicker tissue, at an SID of about 60 to 80 cm
Compression
Power and manual modes must both reach 25 to 40 lb and hold at least 15 seconds, and 40 lb must never be exceeded automatically. Thinner even tissue means less scatter, less motion, a shorter OID, lower dose
Grids and AEC
Grids of 4:1 or 5:1 at 30 to 50 lines per cm; the AEC detector sits behind the receptor and reads intensity and quality
Digital detectors and DBT
TFT arrays with thallium-activated cesium iodide, or a CCD; film-screen still edges them on spatial resolution. Digital breast tomosynthesis sweeps the tube through an arc and reconstructs slices, adding gantry motion and arc calibration to QC
QC schedule
Processor or detector daily, phantom image weekly, visual checklist monthly, repeat analysis quarterly or every 250 patients, compression at least semiannually, medical physicist survey annually or after a major component change
ACR phantom scoring
Count largest to smallest; the minimum to pass accreditation is four fibers, three speck groups, and three masses, and a score must not fall more than 0.5 from the last image
Gantry and slip ring
Tube and detector array rotate together; the slip ring carries power and signals so rotation never stops
Helical scanning and pitch
The couch moves while the gantry turns, tracing a spiral. Pitch is couch travel per rotation over beam width, such as 1.0:1; above 1 the spiral stretches and dose falls, below 1 it overlaps and dose rises
HU scale
Hounsfield units run from -1000 to +3000: air -1000, water exactly 0 by continuous calibration, dense bone about +3000. A water-phantom drift is why numbers go wrong
Cooling and reconstruction
CT tubes carry huge heat loads, so cooling and the heat-unit budget govern how fast a schedule runs; raw data is reconstructed then windowed for display
What the technician services
Table motion and alignment, laser lights, slip-ring brushes, detector and air calibrations, chillers and filters, console and reconstruction computers, and the network link
How it works
A probe's piezoelectric elements turn an electrical pulse into sound and the echo back into a voltage; no ionizing radiation
Frequency and depth
Higher frequency gives finer detail but less penetration; sound also weakens with depth and is blocked by bone and gas, so gel and window matter
Probe types
Linear for superficial work, curved for abdomen and obstetrics, phased array for cardiac, TEE down the esophagus, plus intracavity probes
Doppler
Measures motion and flow from the frequency shift of the echo; noise and poor contact ruin it first
HLD
Probes touching mucous membranes need high-level disinfection between patients; the wrong chemical or a soaked connector destroys a probe
Dropout and service
A dead element or broken cable wire leaves a dark stripe down the image that does not move with the probe. Service covers probes and connectors, cart power and batteries, display and controls, and the network link
Gamma camera chain
Collimator, NaI scintillation crystal, light guide, PMT array, position and energy circuits, then the computer
Technetium-99m (Tc-99m)
The workhorse tracer; it decays to technetium-99 emitting a 140 keV gamma ray, the window the camera is peaked for
PET and hybrids
Positron emitters annihilate with electrons and send out a pair of photons of about 0.51 MeV in opposite directions, and the ring counts coincidences. SPECT/CT and PET/CT add a CT gantry for attenuation correction and anatomy
Instruments and service
Doses are assayed in a dose calibrator and contamination found with survey meters, both calibrated and logged. The technician handles detectors and collimators, PMT tuning and uniformity, gantry motion, computers and links
Magnet
A superconducting coil in a liquid-helium bath, measured in tesla, commonly 3 T, always on
Gradients and RF coils
Gradient coils bend the field to encode position and make the banging noise; RF coils transmit and receive the signal
Cold chain
Compressor, cold head, and chiller keep the helium cold; a helium level alarm or a warm cold head is an emergency
Shielded room and service
Copper shielding and a filter panel keep outside RF out, and a propped door shows as zipper artifacts. The technician services chillers and compressors, coils and cables, table motion, rated peripherals, and the console side

PM, QC, and test equipment 33

Mechanical
Locks, brakes, detents, counterweights, cables and chains, bearing play, tube stand and rails, table travel, collision sensors; plus filters, fans, dust, and room temperature, because heat kills generators and detectors
Electrical safety
Ground resistance 0.5 ohm maximum and chassis leakage within the limit your facility cites, with an analyzer, at incoming inspection, after repair, and on schedule
Interlocks
Door, rotor ready, receptor parked, collimator, emergency stops: prove each one blocks the exposure
Radiation output
kVp accuracy, timer, linearity, reproducibility, HVL, and leakage on the schedule the state and the manufacturer set
Logs and documentation
Read the error log every visit, note firmware versions, record before clearing, patch only on the vendor's validated schedule, and close the work order with the measured value, the tolerance, and pass or fail
kVp accuracy
Measured kVp within 10 percent of the indicated kVp
Exposure timer accuracy
Within 5 percent of the indicated time above 10 ms; 20 percent at 10 ms or less
Linearity and reproducibility
No more than 10 percent variation in output per mAs between adjacent mA stations, and no more than plus or minus 5 percent over repeated identical exposures
Collimation and beam alignment
Light field and x-ray field within 2 percent of the SID, with PBL and the SID indicator held to the same 2 percent
HVL
Measure and compare with the minimum for that kVp and waveform; meeting it proves the filtration is adequate
Focal spot size
Pinhole camera, star pattern, or slit camera against the nominal size and its variance
AEC performance
Constant density through varying thicknesses of aluminum or acrylic, plus a backup timer test at 6 s or 600 mAs
When to retest
Annually, after major repair to the console or high-voltage generator, and whenever output looks wrong
Tabletop exposure rate and timer
A chamber at the tabletop against the 10 R/min and 20 R/min limits, and the audible signal at 5 minutes
Geometry
SSD at least 38 cm stationary or 30 cm mobile with the spacer in place, and an unexposed border with the input phosphor 35 cm above the tabletop
Image quality
A resolution and low-contrast phantom at fixed geometry against the baseline on file
Daily and weekly
Processor or detector check and cleanliness daily; phantom image, screen cleanliness, viewing conditions weekly
Monthly and quarterly
Visual checklist monthly; repeat analysis quarterly or every 250 patients
Semiannual and annual
Compression force at least semiannually; medical physicist survey annually or after a major component change
Phantom scan
Depth of penetration, resolution, and uniformity at fixed settings against the baseline
Probe, display, and controls
Cracks in the lens, kinked cables, bent connector pins, and chemical damage; brightness and contrast against the test pattern, with every control and footswitch working
Non-invasive kVp meter
Reads kVp, time, dose, dose rate, and HVL from outside the beam path, and verifies time and mAs independently of the console
Ionization chamber and solid-state detector
The reference dose and dose-rate detectors for output, fluoroscopic rate, and leakage
DAP meter
Measures dose area product under the collimator, tracking dose and the volume of tissue irradiated
Phantoms, filters, test tools
Calibrated aluminum sheets added until intensity halves give the HVL; plus resolution and contrast phantoms, the beam-alignment tool, pinhole and star patterns, and the mammography and CT accreditation phantoms
Staff dosimeters
TLD and OSL badges read by a service, plus direct-reading electronic dosimeters; worn at the collar outside the apron
DMM or DVM
Voltage, current, and resistance at the test points the manual names; on continuity an OL reading means the path is open
Electrical safety analyzer
Ground resistance and leakage against the NFPA 99 and IEC 60601-1 limits, in normal, reversed-polarity, and open-ground conditions
Dose calibrator
Assays activity in nuclear medicine before a dose is given, with its own constancy, accuracy, linearity, and geometry tests
Inventory and PM record
The CMMS: complete, current, risk-classified, with completion rates and reasons for anything overdue
QC logs
Signed, dated records with readings and tolerances, technologist daily checks included
Physicist and safety reports
Annual surveys with findings and closure dates, dosimetry reports, committee minutes, shielding designs
Recalls and training
Each notice with the devices affected and what was done, and who is competent on what, contractors included

Troubleshooting imaging systems 20

Patient and staff safety
Stop the exposure, lock out the room, remove the device from service; an unsafe machine never stays in use to protect a schedule
Clinical downtime
A down room reroutes patients; say when it will be back and give radiology a workaround
Compliance
The repair is not done until the test, the record, and the sign-off are done
Convenience
Cosmetic items wait, but write them down so they are not lost
No exposure
With no error code it is an interlock: door, rotor not ready, receptor not parked or wrong size, collimator, emergency stop. Follow the series chain until a contact is open. With a fault code, read the code and the log: tube arc, overcurrent, line voltage, thermal cutout, failed contactor
Output low or high
Verify kVp and timer with a meter, check mA linearity and filtration, then the AEC cell and density setting. Burnt-out images point at a timer or AEC failure or calibration lost after a board swap; density differing between stations is a linearity fault
Rotor will not spin or runs noisy
Stator drive, capacitor, or bearing wear; a noisy rotor with a slow run-up means the tube is near its end
Artifacts
Grid lines mean a stationary grid or a Bucky not moving. Cutoff names the error: upside down fades the edges, off level drops density everywhere, off center drops it at the sides. On digital, stripes mean a stale gain or pixel map, a ghost means an incomplete CR erase, moire means grid frequency beating against detector sampling, repeating marks mean a scored plate
Mechanical drift, drop, collision
Locks and detents out of adjustment, worn cable or counterweight, failed collision sensor; a safety fault, not a comfort item
Dim or noisy image
ABC at its limit, an aging intensifier losing gain, a camera or flat-panel fault, or a very large patient; compare dose rate with the baseline first. Image rotation or edge distortion is intensifier aging, which flat panels do not do
Dose rate too high
ABC calibration, a magnification mode left engaged, continuous instead of pulsed mode, or a missing filter; measure at the tabletop against the 10 R/min and 20 R/min limits
Compression will not reach or hold
Paddle, drive, or force calibration; verify 25 to 40 lb in both modes with a scale and that 40 lb cannot be exceeded automatically
Images too light or dark, or the phantom score falls
AEC detector position, cell selection, or detector calibration; confirm with a phantom image before touching technique. A drop of more than 0.5 means stop and investigate calibration, target and filter selection, compression, or processing
Filter wheel fault or repeating artifacts
The wheel motor, position sensor, or interlock behind a target or filter error; a mark in the same place every image is a detector or plate defect, dust in the beam path, or a damaged paddle
Dark stripe down the image
Element dropout or a broken cable conductor; confirm on a phantom, then swap the probe to prove it
Weak or noisy image, or absent Doppler
Wrong preset, poor contact and gel, lens or connector damage, or a failing channel; try a known good probe first. A dead display or control is cart power, battery, cable, or the panel
Probe damage after cleaning
A disinfectant not approved for that probe, soaking past the immersion line, or a soaked connector; retrain and relabel
Will not expose away from mains, or dies within a shift
Battery capacity under load, charger fault, a charge interlock, or a unit stored discharged; measure the pack under load and log run time
Drive, brakes, or faults that follow movement
Brake pads, drive belt, wheel bearings, or dead-man drive switch; faults that follow arm movement are cable flex failures, found with a wiggle test on continuity
Collimator lamp or laser out
Lamp, timer circuit, or mirror alignment; a dark lamp invites an uncollimated field, so it is a dose issue

Imaging informatics 27

IP address, subnet mask, gateway
Four numbers 0 to 255 name the device; the mask splits that into network and host, and two devices must share a subnet to talk without a router. The default gateway is the way out, and a wrong one looks like the whole network is down from that device
DHCP and DNS
DHCP hands out addresses, and a self-assigned 169.254 address means it could not be reached. DNS turns names into addresses: if the address works and the name does not, it is DNS
Switch versus router
A switch connects devices inside one LAN; a router connects networks and usually carries the access rules
VLAN
A logical network on shared switches. Imaging gear often sits on its own VLAN, which is why a good cable in the wrong port gets nowhere
LAN, WAN, and wireless
The LAN is the building and the WAN joins sites, where slow prior retrievals live. Fixed modalities are wired; portables roam, so coverage gaps leave studies stuck in the local queue
Cabling and NIC
Cat 5e for 1 Gbps, Cat 6A for 10 Gbps, 100 m per run, RJ45 connectors, fiber for long runs. No link light on the network card is a layer 1 problem, cable or port
PING and traceroute
PING sends ICMP echoes, and a reply proves the path and host are alive: work outward from own address to gateway to archive by address to archive by name. traceroute shows each router hop and where the path stops, which matters across a WAN before blaming the modality
ipconfig or ifconfig
Reads the device's own address, mask, gateway, and DNS: the fastest way to spot a bad address
Cable tester, tracer, port lights
Prove the pairs end to end and find which jack is which; lights on both ends settle the physical layer
DICOM echo
A C-ECHO verifies the association, AE titles, address, and port: the DICOM ping, and the first test when images will not move
Association, AE title, host, port
Two application entities negotiate an association and must agree on who they are and what services they support. Each node answers to a case-sensitive AE title plus address and port, commonly 104 or 11112; a typo here is the most common reason a new room cannot send
SOP class
The service and object pair that says what a node can do, such as store a CT image or query a worklist
C-ECHO and C-STORE
Verification, then the push that sends images to the archive. A node that verifies but cannot store usually has a class mismatch, or a disk, license, or permission limit at the receiver
C-FIND and C-MOVE
Query for matching studies, then ask a node to send them somewhere; retrieving priors needs the destination configured on the sending node
MWL and MPPS
The modality worklist query pulls scheduled patients and accession numbers to the console; performed procedure step reports started, completed, or discontinued, which drives status boards and billing
Storage commitment and GSDF
Storage commitment is the archive confirming permanent responsibility, which makes local deletion safe; the grayscale standard display function is the calibration curve that makes an image look the same on every reading station
PACS and VNA
The archive plus reading workstations store, retrieve, distribute, and display. A vendor neutral archive holds studies from many systems in a standard form, so a vendor can be replaced without migrating the data again
RIS
Schedules exams, holds the worklist, tracks status, routes reports
HL7
The messaging standard joining those systems: ADT for admit, discharge, and transfer, ORM for orders, ORU for results and reports
Order to report
Ordered in the EMR, scheduled in the RIS, shown on the modality as a worklist entry, images to PACS, read and dictated, report back to the EMR and the EHR clinicians read
Interface engine or broker
Translates and routes HL7 and DICOM traffic between systems; its queue is where stuck messages pile up
HIPAA, HITECH, and PHI
HIPAA protects PHI through its privacy, security, and breach rules; HITECH strengthened enforcement, added breach notification, and bound service vendors. Identifiers sit in consoles, caches, dose reports, and service logs, so sanitize or document before a device leaves the building
MDS2
The manufacturer disclosure statement for medical device security: what a device stores, how it authenticates, and what it can be patched with
IEC 80001
Risk management for IT networks carrying medical devices: the framework behind joint reviews with the IT department
Least privilege and remote access
Separate service and clinical accounts, no shared logins, vendor access through the hospital VPN with a controlled account, logged and time-limited, never an always-on modem
Patching, segmentation, encryption
Patch only on the vendor's validated schedule; a modality that cannot be patched is segmented onto its own VLAN with only the ports it needs; encrypt anything leaving the building
Backups
Archives and databases backed up and restore-tested; a backup nobody has restored is a hope, not a plan
